title: Molokai History Project - Mid Nite Inn: Talk Story with John & Philip Kikukawa

issues.title: Proposed Maui County passenger ferry to Molokaʻi and Lānaʻi

recap.headline: Molokaʻi talk story recalls the Midnight Inn and plantation-era island life
recap.in_60_seconds: The Molokaʻi History Project hosted a recorded talk story with two brothers whose family ran the Midnight Inn restaurant in Kaunakakai. They shared memories of growing up in the restaurant, their grandmother's start with a saimin stand, their father's service in the 442nd, and plantation-era jobs and businesses. About seven people spoke, including audience members who worked at the inn or grew up nearby. Speakers raised concerns about newcomers who do not connect with the community, youth fights between parts of the island, development pressure and whether ferry service will return. No decisions were made, and participants said they would like to hold more sessions like this.

parts.title: Welcome and opening prayer
presented: The host introduced two brothers whose family ran the Midnight Inn, which she called a gathering spot for politicians and residents.
An audience member offered an opening prayer.

parts.title: Childhood near the restaurant
parts.presenter: Featured speakers, two brothers from the restaurant family
presented: The brothers grew up about half a mile from the restaurant in a Molokaʻi Ranch rental camp.
They recalled black, smelly shoreline mud from fuel and waste oil that drained from a power plant pipe.
Families evacuated to the armory during tidal wave warnings.
Plantation workers were housed in separate camps by ethnicity, which they said was meant to discourage unionizing.

parts.title: Growing up in the Midnight Inn and family history
parts.presenter: Featured speakers, two brothers from the restaurant family
presented: The restaurant was the brothers' playground and had a four-lane bowling alley with pin boys.
A soda fountain drew young people until it closed when their grandmother stopped helping.
Their grandmother started the business and also ran a florist business with orchid hothouses.
Their grandfather was a contractor who built several Kaunakakai buildings, including the building that is now the fire station.

parts.title: Politicians, the 442nd and the war
parts.presenter: Featured speakers, two brothers from the restaurant family
presented: Senator Inouye and other leaders visited the restaurant, which the brothers called the island's central social point.
Their father left the University of Hawaiʻi to join the 442nd and came home with a wartime injury.
Their mother came after the war as a teacher from the East Coast.
An audience member who recently visited Normandy spoke about honoring veterans.

parts.title: Running the restaurant and plantation work
parts.presenter: Featured speakers, two brothers from the restaurant family
presented: Staff almost tripled by the early 1980s as Molokaʻi got busier.
The name came from late-night meals served to dock workers unloading steamships near midnight.
One brother earned $125 a week as a pineapple field luna.
They recalled four movie theaters and many gas stations on the island.

parts.title: Change on Molokaʻi and welcoming newcomers
presented: Speakers said Molokaʻi has a code built on aloha and talking story.
An audience member told a story of a Hawaiian family in Hoʻolehua who took in a Japanese immigrant family.

raised.concern: Some newcomers live in their own bubble and do not learn local ways or greet neighbors.
Young people are confused by instant information that is not always true and need to be taught by elders.

parts.title: Surfing, rivalries and old Kaunakakai
presented: Surfing let one brother get to know people across the island at a time when neighborhoods were territorial.
Participants listed businesses that once lined Kaunakakai, including two pool halls and a bakery.
The class of 1973 wore Hawaiian attire instead of caps and gowns at graduation.

raised.concern: Fights between youth from different parts of the island still happen.
Kaunakakai no longer has Christmas lights like it used to.

parts.title: Airlines, development pressure and the ferry
presented: Up to about five airlines served Molokaʻi, and one fare was as low as $9.
A speaker said Molokaʻi once had more landings than other islands because of training flights.
One airline flew 600 passengers on one Memorial Day weekend.

raised.concern: Cheaper real estate is drawing outside investment and development to Molokaʻi.
The island needs a central place to record its history, since the existing museum focuses on one family.
Ferry service may not start again.

answered.said: He said the state had known about the ferry issue for decades and that recovery spending after the Lahaina fire could slow such efforts, or a change of administration could stop them.

parts.title: Closing remarks
presented: One brother left early because of a family emergency.
Participants thanked the speakers and acknowledged long-time Hawaiian families in the room.

next.what: Hold another talk story session with more old-timers

open_questions.question: Will passenger ferry service to Molokaʻi start again?

not_on_tracker.topic: Newcomers connecting with the Molokaʻi community
not_on_tracker.why: Speakers said the island's way of life depends on people greeting, helping and talking story with each other.

not_on_tracker.topic: Youth rivalries between parts of Molokaʻi
not_on_tracker.why: Participants were surprised and saddened that fights between areas still happen on such a small island.
A speaker said the town once felt more vibrant and the community should figure out how to bring the lights back.

not_on_tracker.topic: Development pressure and real estate prices
not_on_tracker.why: A speaker said Molokaʻi is now the last island drawing outside investment, which could change its character.
A speaker welcomed the project because no central place records the whole island's history.
